# Crumbly

Crumbly builds breadcrumb trails for Rails apps. A breadcrumb trail is the line of links at the top of a page that
shows where it sits in the site:

```
Home › Customers › Alice › Orders › Order 2026-0042
```

You describe each level once, as a Ruby method that names its parent. Most pages need nothing more: when a view
doesn't say which trail it wants, Crumbly works it out from the controller, the action and the routes. A test
checks every trail in the app, so a broken one fails CI before anyone opens the page.

The guide, the migration notes and the benchmarks are also on the website: <https://levups.github.io/crumbly/>.

Coding agents can start from <https://levups.github.io/crumbly/llms.txt>, or read this README and the
website's pages as one Markdown file: <https://levups.github.io/crumbly/llms-full.txt>.

## Why Crumbly

Crumbly was written to replace [gretel](https://github.com/kzkn/gretel) in a back office with 265 crumbs, in one
file of about 1,000 lines, and 380 calls in views. It works differently in a few ways:

- The crumbs of each part of the app live in their own class, `Admin::Breadcrumbs` or `Storefront::Breadcrumbs`,
  so the admin and the storefront can both have an `orders` crumb.
- A crumb is a plain method. Route helpers work in it as in a view, and a backtrace points at its line.
- Index, show, new and edit pages get their trail from the routes and the record the controller loaded, so most
  views name no crumb.
- One test reads every crumb and fails on a parent, a route helper or a crumb name that doesn't exist, without
  touching the database.
- The trail comes back as data, and your layout writes the HTML. The gem has no styles or rendering options.
- Rendering a five-level trail as an `<ol>` takes 45.4 µs against 57.6 µs for gretel, with 274 allocations
  instead of 345 (YJIT off). JSON-LD is a little slower: see [Performance](https://github.com/levups/crumbly#performance).

Its runtime dependencies are Action Pack, Active Support and Loofah, which Rails already installs.

## Installation

Add the gem to your Gemfile:

```ruby
gem "crumbly"
```

It needs Ruby 3.3 or later and Rails 8.0 or later. There is nothing to configure: the gem adds `breadcrumb`,
`breadcrumb_trail` and `breadcrumb_json_ld` to your views, and `breadcrumbs_with` to your controllers.

## Getting started

### 1. Write the crumbs

Crumbs live in a class that inherits from `Crumbly::Trail`. Every public method in it is a crumb. A crumb returns
a label and a URL, and its parent if it has one:

```ruby
# app/breadcrumbs/admin/breadcrumbs.rb
module Admin
  class Breadcrumbs < Crumbly::Trail
    def root
      crumb "Home", admin_root_path
    end

    def orders
      crumb "Orders", admin_orders_path
    end

    def order(order)
      crumb order.to_s, admin_order_path(order), parent: orders
    end
  end
end
```

The parent of `order` is the result of calling `orders`, so the trail of an order page is Home › Orders ›
Order 42. When `root` exists, every trail starts with it. Your route helpers work inside the class as they do in
a view. Rails loads the file like any other in `app/`, so `app/breadcrumbs/admin/breadcrumbs.rb` defines
`Admin::Breadcrumbs`.

### 2. Render the trail in the layout

`breadcrumb_trail` returns the levels of the current page, from the root to the page itself. Each level has a
`label`, a `url` and `current?`, which is true for the last one. The HTML is up to you:

```erb
<%# app/views/layouts/admin.html.erb %>
<nav aria-label="Breadcrumb">
  <ol>
    <% breadcrumb_trail.each do |level| %>
      <li><%= link_to_unless level.current?, level.label, level.url %></li>
    <% end %>
  </ol>
</nav>
```

On the page of an order whose `to_s` is "Order 42", with the admin routes at `/admin`, this writes:

```html
<nav aria-label="Breadcrumb">
  <ol>
    <li><a href="/admin">Home</a></li>
    <li><a href="/admin/orders">Orders</a></li>
    <li>Order 42</li>
  </ol>
</nav>
```

### 3. Pick a crumb in a view, when you need to

A view can name the crumb it wants:

```erb
<%# app/views/admin/orders/show.html.erb %>
<% breadcrumb @order %>
```

`breadcrumb @order` calls the crumb named after the record's model, `order` for an `Order`. To call a crumb by
name, write `breadcrumb :orders`, and pass its arguments after the name (`breadcrumb :order, @order`).

In this example the line isn't needed. A `show` page with no `breadcrumb` call already gets the trail of its
record (see [Trails Crumbly works out on its own](https://github.com/levups/crumbly#trails-crumbly-works-out-on-its-own)).

## Writing crumbs

A crumb calls `crumb label, url = nil, parent: nil, links: []`.

`url` can be a string, a record or a polymorphic array such as `[:admin, owner, :returns]`. Leave it out for a
level without a link. A `javascript:`, `vbscript:` or `data:` URL would run a script once your layout links it,
so Crumbly refuses it, however it is spelled (`" JavaScript:"`, `"java\tscript:"`): see
[Mistakes in development and in production](https://github.com/levups/crumbly#mistakes-in-development-and-in-production).

`links:` is for a level that points to more than one page. It takes extra `link(label, url)` entries, which your
layout reads from `level.links`.

`crumb_for(record)` finds the crumb of a record from its model. Use it when the parent can be one of several
models:

```ruby
def returns(owner = nil)
  return crumb("Returns", admin_returns_path) unless owner

  crumb "Returns", [:admin, owner, :returns], parent: crumb_for(owner)
end
```

For a single-table inheritance subclass that has no crumb of its own, `crumb_for` and `breadcrumb @record` use the
crumb of its parent class.

Private methods are helpers, not crumbs, so you can put shared code in them. View helpers such as `t` or
`current_user` are reached through `helpers`: `helpers.t(".orders")`.

Any public method can be called from a view, so `Crumbly::Trail` keeps its own methods private. Don't name a crumb
`crumb`, `link`, `crumb_for` or `helpers`.

## One trail class per namespace

`Admin::OrdersController` uses `Admin::Breadcrumbs`. If there is none, Crumbly looks in the enclosing modules,
then for a top-level `Breadcrumbs`. An admin area and a storefront can each have an `orders` crumb, and they
don't clash.

A controller outside the namespace picks its class with `breadcrumbs_with`:

```ruby
class CheckoutController < ApplicationController
  breadcrumbs_with Storefront::Breadcrumbs
end
```

## Trails Crumbly works out on its own

When a view doesn't call `breadcrumb`, Crumbly builds the trail from the action:

| Action | Trail |
|---|---|
| `index` | the collection: your `posts` crumb if you wrote one, or else the model's plural name linked to the `index` route |
| `show` | the record: your `post` crumb, or else its label linked to the `show` route, under the collection |
| `new`, `create` | "New" under the collection |
| `edit`, `update` | "Edit" under the record |

The record is the one the controller has already loaded, `@post` in `PostsController`. Crumbly never runs a query
to find it. "New" and "Edit" come from the `crumbly.new` and `crumbly.edit` translations, so you can translate
them. A record's label is its `to_s`. A model without a `to_s` of its own gets its translated model name and id
instead ("Post 5"), not `#<Post:0x000...>`.

Nested routes work too. On `/admin/posts/5/comments`, the trail is Posts › Post 5 › Comments, and the post is
the `@post` the controller loaded. If the controller didn't load it, Crumbly skips that level and keeps Posts.

To change how these trails are built, override the private methods `collection_crumb`, `record_crumb`,
`new_record_crumb` or `edit_record_crumb` in your trail class.

To turn them off, set `derive_trails false` in the trail class. A view that doesn't call `breadcrumb` then has no
trail, as with gretel: `breadcrumb_trail` returns `[]` and `breadcrumb_json_ld` returns `nil`.

```ruby
module Admin
  class Breadcrumbs < Crumbly::Trail
    derive_trails false
  end
end
```

Subclasses inherit the setting, and `derive_trails true` turns it back on in one of them.

### Which crumb wins

Crumbly takes the first of these that applies:

1. The crumb the view names with `breadcrumb`.
2. Your crumb named after the controller: `posts` in `Admin::PostsController#index`. Under a nested route it is
   named after the whole nesting and gets the parent records, so `/admin/orders/42/messages` calls
   `order_messages(order)`. On `show` and `edit`, it is the crumb named after the record's model (`post`).
3. The trail Crumbly works out. Its parent levels follow the same rule: your crumb for the parent's model if there
   is one, or else a level Crumbly builds.

With `derive_trails false`, only the first applies.

## Testing your trails

Add one test:

```ruby
# test/breadcrumbs_test.rb
require "test_helper"
require "crumbly/test_helper"

class BreadcrumbsTest < ActiveSupport::TestCase
  test "breadcrumbs" do
    assert_breadcrumbs_valid
  end
end
```

It loads the whole app and reads the source of every crumb, without running them or touching the database. It
fails when:

- a crumb's parent is not a crumb, or a `_path` or `_url` it calls is not a route helper;
- a `breadcrumb :name` in `app/views` or `app/controllers` names a crumb that no trail class defines;
- a view or another crumb calls a crumb with the wrong number of arguments (calls spread over several lines, or
  with a splat, are skipped);
- a crumb is never used. A crumb is used when another crumb, a view or a controller calls it, when a trail
  Crumbly works out reads it (unless its class sets `derive_trails false`), or when it is named after a model.

A crumb defined twice in the same class is caught even earlier: the class raises `Crumbly::DuplicateCrumb` when it
loads.

Outside Minitest, `Crumbly.verify!` runs the same checks. It raises `Crumbly::InvalidTrail` with every problem in
one message, and returns the unused crumbs (`["Admin::Breadcrumbs#drafts"]`). Both accept `trail_classes:`,
`routes:` and `sources:`, the directories it scans for `breadcrumb` calls.

## Mistakes in development and in production

A view that asks for a crumb that doesn't exist raises `Crumbly::UnknownCrumb` in development and test. So does
`breadcrumb @order` when `@order` is `nil`. In production the error goes to `Rails.error`, and the page renders
without a trail instead of failing.

A crumb whose URL a browser would run as a script raises `Crumbly::UnsafeUrl` in development and test. In
production the error goes to `Rails.error`, and the level keeps its label without the link.

To raise in production too, on a staging server for example, set either in an initializer:

```ruby
# config/initializers/crumbly.rb
Crumbly.raise_on_unknown_crumb = true # on staging too
Crumbly.raise_on_unsafe_url = true
```

## Breadcrumbs for search engines

Google can show a page's trail in its results when the page describes it as schema.org structured data.
`breadcrumb_json_ld` writes that description for the current trail. Put it in the `<head>`:

```erb
<%# app/views/layouts/storefront.html.erb %>
<%= breadcrumb_json_ld %>
```

Google needs absolute URLs, so use `_url` helpers in the crumbs of that namespace:

```ruby
module Storefront
  class Breadcrumbs < Crumbly::Trail
    def category(category)
      crumb category.name, storefront_category_url(category),
        parent: category.parent ? category(category.parent) : shop
    end
  end
end
```

A relative URL raises `Crumbly::RelativeUrl` in development and test. In production it is reported to
`Rails.error` and the page has no structured data. `Crumbly.raise_on_relative_url` changes this.

Some details of the output:

- Positions start at 1. The last level may have no URL. A level above it without a URL isn't a page, so it is
  left out.
- Names are plain text. If a label is `html_safe` (an icon, a `<b>`), its tags are removed.
- The JSON is escaped for a `<script>` tag, so a label can't close it.
- `Crumbly::JsonLd.call(levels)` returns the same data as a hash, if you build the structured data of the page
  yourself.

## Switching from gretel, loaf or breadcrumbs_on_rails

Crumbly uses the same view helper names as these gems, so an app switches in one go: there is no compatibility
layer, and the old gem leaves the Gemfile once the migration is merged.

From gretel, the calls in your views barely change (`breadcrumb :order, @order` and `breadcrumb @order` work as
before), and `crumbly-convert` turns `config/breadcrumbs.rb` into a trail class:

```sh
bundle exec crumbly-convert config/breadcrumbs.rb --namespace Admin \
  --output app/breadcrumbs/admin/breadcrumbs.rb --views app/views/admin
```

It prints each line it left out or couldn't convert exactly, and with `--views`, the `breadcrumb` calls that
Crumbly may now make unnecessary. It needs Prism 1.2 or later: Ruby 3.4 comes with it, and on Ruby 3.3 you add
`gem "prism"` to the development group. While gretel is still installed on the migration branch,
`Crumbly::Oracle` draws each trail your tests render with both gems and lists where the labels or URLs differ.
To keep gretel's empty trail on pages whose views name no crumb, set `derive_trails false` in the trail class.

The [migration guide](https://levups.github.io/crumbly/migration.html) has every step: what the converter maps to
what, what it leaves to you, the comparison in your tests, and the same walk-through for loaf and
breadcrumbs_on_rails. The [home page](https://levups.github.io/crumbly/) shows five crumbs from a real gretel app
next to their Crumbly version.

## Performance

`bench/render.rb` renders the same five-level trail (Home > Customers > Alice > Orders > Order 2026-0042) with
gretel and with Crumbly, and checks that both give the same output. The `<ol>` row compares gretel's
`breadcrumbs(style: :ol)` with a ten-line helper over `breadcrumb_trail`. The JSON-LD row compares gretel's
`structured_data(url_base:)`, with paths behind a prefix, and `breadcrumb_json_ld` with `_url` helpers. Both are
encoded and escaped the same way.

Ruby 4.0.9, Rails 8.1.4, gretel 5.1.0, Apple M5 (arm64 macOS), median of three runs of benchmark-ips:

| Render | Allocations | Time, YJIT off | Time, YJIT on |
|---|---|---|---|
| gretel `<ol>` | 345 | 57.6 µs | 35.1 µs |
| Crumbly `<ol>` | 274 | 45.4 µs | 29.8 µs |
| gretel JSON-LD | 268 | 41.3 µs | 25.4 µs |
| Crumbly JSON-LD | 287 | 43.3 µs | 29.5 µs |

Crumbly's JSON-LD is a little slower, mostly because Rails' `_url` helpers are slower than `_path` ones. Building
the `BreadcrumbList` from the levels takes 1.7 µs of the difference.

```sh
bundle exec ruby bench/render.rb
bundle exec ruby --yjit bench/render.rb
```

## How Crumbly is tested

CI runs the test suite on Ruby 3.3, 3.4 and 4.0, each against Rails 8.0 and 8.1, and on `ruby-head`. The
tests convert a sample gretel file, compare the result with the expected class line for line, then draw its trails
with gretel and with the converted class and check that the labels and URLs match. The production paths (an unknown crumb, a relative JSON-LD URL) are tested
as well as the raising ones.

## Development

```sh
bundle install
bundle exec rake test                                            # latest Rails
BUNDLE_GEMFILE=gemfiles/rails_8_0.gemfile bundle exec rake test  # Rails 8.0
bundle exec rubocop
bundle exec rake docs:highlight                                  # after editing a code block in docs/
bundle exec rake docs:llms                                       # after editing the README or docs/
```

[CONTRIBUTING.md](https://github.com/levups/crumbly/blob/main/CONTRIBUTING.md) says what a pull request needs.

### Releasing

Pull requests don't touch `CHANGELOG.md`. A release starts by writing its notes under `## [Unreleased]`, from the
pull requests merged since the last tag, without committing them. Then, from an up-to-date `main` with green CI:

```sh
bin/release minor --dry-run   # shows the notes and the changes, writes nothing
bin/release minor             # or patch, major, or an exact version such as 1.2.0
```

`main` takes no direct push, so `bin/release` dates the notes and bumps the version on a `release/vX.Y.Z` branch,
opens a pull request that merges itself once CI is green, and waits for it (`bin/release --wait X.Y.Z` if you
stopped it). The merge starts the Release workflow, which waits for a maintainer's approval, tags the merge commit
`vX.Y.Z`, publishes the gem to RubyGems through trusted publishing and creates the GitHub release with the notes
and the `.gem`.

MIT, by Level UP Solutions. The idea of a crumb that names its parent comes from
[gretel](https://github.com/kzkn/gretel), by Lasse Bunk and Kazuki Nishikawa.

## Crumbly Guide

<https://levups.github.io/crumbly/guide.html>

How to write crumbs and render the trail, what Crumbly does when a view names no crumb, and how to test it all.

### Installation

```ruby
# Gemfile
gem "crumbly"
```

There is nothing to configure: the gem adds `breadcrumb`, `breadcrumb_trail` and `breadcrumb_json_ld` to your views, and `breadcrumbs_with` to your controllers. It needs Ruby 3.3 or later and Rails 8.0 or later.

### Writing crumbs

Crumbs live in a class that inherits from `Crumbly::Trail`. Every public method in it is a crumb. A crumb returns a label and a URL, and its parent if it has one, which is a call to another crumb. Rails loads the class like any other file in `app/`, so `app/breadcrumbs/admin/breadcrumbs.rb` defines `Admin::Breadcrumbs`.

```ruby
# app/breadcrumbs/admin/breadcrumbs.rb
module Admin
  class Breadcrumbs < Crumbly::Trail
    def root
      crumb "Home", admin_root_path
    end

    def orders
      crumb "Orders", admin_orders_path
    end

    def order(order)
      crumb order.to_s, admin_order_path(order), parent: orders
    end

    def order_documents(order)
      crumb "Documents", nil, parent: order(order),
        links: [link("Invoices", admin_order_invoices_path(order)), link("Receipts", admin_order_receipts_path(order))]
    end
  end
end
```

```erb
<%# app/views/admin/orders/show.html.erb: optional, this is what the trail derives on its own %>
<% breadcrumb @order %>
```

#### In a view

- `breadcrumb :orders` calls the crumb named `orders`. Its arguments come after the name: `breadcrumb :order, @order`.
- `breadcrumb @order` calls the crumb named after the record's model, `order` for an `Order`. For a single-table inheritance subclass that has no crumb of its own, it uses the crumb of its parent class. A `nil` record, when the controller hasn't loaded `@order`, counts as an unknown crumb.
- A view that calls neither gets a trail Crumbly [works out on its own](https://levups.github.io/crumbly/guide.html#derived).

#### In a trail class

| Method | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| `crumb label, url = nil, parent: nil, links: []` | One level. `url` can be a string, a record or a polymorphic array such as `[:admin, owner, :returns]`. Leave it out for a level without a link. A `javascript:`, `vbscript:` or `data:` URL would run a script once your layout links it, so Crumbly refuses it, however it is spelled: see [`Crumbly::UnsafeUrl`](https://levups.github.io/crumbly/guide.html#errors). |
| `link label, url` | An extra link for `links:`, when a level points to more than one page. |
| `crumb_for record` | The crumb of a record, found from its model. Use it when the parent can be one of several models. |
| `helpers` | The view, for view helpers such as `helpers.t(".orders")` or `helpers.current_user`. |
| `root` | Yours to define. When it exists, every trail starts with it. |

Private methods are helpers, not crumbs, so you can put shared code in them. Any public method can be called from a view, so `Crumbly::Trail` keeps its own methods private. Don't name a crumb `crumb`, `link`, `crumb_for` or `helpers`.

### Rendering the trail

`breadcrumb_trail` returns the levels of the current page, from the root to the page itself. Each level has a `label`, a `url` (a path, or `nil`), its extra `links` (each with a `label` and a `url`), and `current?`, which is true for the last one. The gem writes no HTML for you. Whether the current page is a link, which separator to use and how to show extra links are up to your layout:

```erb
<%# app/views/layouts/admin.html.erb %>
<nav aria-label="Breadcrumb">
  <ol>
    <% breadcrumb_trail.each do |level| %>
      <li>
        <%= link_to_unless level.current?, level.label, level.url %>
        <% level.links.each do |link| %>
          <%= link_to link.label, link.url %>
        <% end %>
      </li>
    <% end %>
  </ol>
</nav>
```

Rails renders a view before its layout, so a `breadcrumb` call anywhere in the view runs before the layout reads `breadcrumb_trail`.

### One trail class per namespace

`Admin::OrdersController` uses `Admin::Breadcrumbs`. If there is none, Crumbly looks in the enclosing modules, then for a top-level `Breadcrumbs`. An admin area and a storefront can each have an `order` crumb, and they don't clash.

A controller outside the namespace picks its class with `breadcrumbs_with`, and its subclasses inherit the choice:

```ruby
class CheckoutController < ApplicationController
  breadcrumbs_with Storefront::Breadcrumbs
end
```

The classes live in `app/breadcrumbs/`, which Rails autoloads. With eager loading they are in memory before a prefork server forks.

### Trails Crumbly works out on its own

When a view doesn't call `breadcrumb`, Crumbly builds the trail from the action:

| Action | Trail |
| --- | --- |
| `index` | The collection: your `posts` crumb if you wrote one, or else the model's plural name linked to the `index` route. |
| `show` | The record: your `post` crumb, or else its label linked to the `show` route, under the collection. |
| `new`, `create` | "New" under the collection. |
| `edit`, `update` | "Edit" under the record. |

The record is the one the controller has already loaded, `@post` in `PostsController`. Crumbly never runs a query to find it, and without it `show` and `edit` get no trail. A controller with no `index` or `show` route still gets its level, without a link. Other actions get nothing.

#### Labels

A record's label is its `to_s`. A model without a `to_s` of its own gets its model name, translated by `model_name.human`, and its id instead: "Post 5", not `#<Post:0x000...>`.

"New" and "Edit" come from the `crumbly.new` and `crumbly.edit` translations:

```yaml
# config/locales/es.yml
es:
  crumbly:
    new: Nuevo
    edit: Editar
```

#### Overrides

To change how these trails are built in a namespace, override any of four private methods in its trail class: `collection_crumb`, `record_crumb(record)`, `new_record_crumb` and `edit_record_crumb(record)`. The `controller` they read is private too.

```ruby
module Admin
  class Breadcrumbs < Crumbly::Trail
    private

    def new_record_crumb
      crumb helpers.t("admin.breadcrumbs.new"), parent: collection_crumb
    end
  end
end
```

#### Nested routes

Under a nested route, each `:<name>_id` path parameter adds a parent level, outermost first. On `/admin/posts/5/comments`, the trail is Posts › Post 5 › Comments, and the post is the `@post` the controller loaded. Its level is your `post` crumb, or else its label linked to its `show` route.

If the controller didn't load a parent, Crumbly doesn't query it. It skips that level and the crumb named after the nesting, and keeps the parent's collection: Posts › Comments.

#### Turning them off

To draw only the trails your views name, set `derive_trails false` in the trail class. A view that doesn't call `breadcrumb` then has no trail, as with gretel: `breadcrumb_trail` returns `[]` and `breadcrumb_json_ld` returns `nil`.

```ruby
module Admin
  class Breadcrumbs < Crumbly::Trail
    derive_trails false
  end
end
```

Subclasses inherit the setting, and `derive_trails true` turns it back on in one of them. The breadcrumbs test no longer counts a crumb as used because a derived trail would read it, and `Crumbly::Oracle` lists no call as redundant.

### Which crumb wins

Crumbly takes the first of these that applies:

1. The crumb the view names with `breadcrumb`.
2. Your crumb named after the controller: `posts` in `Admin::PostsController#index`. Under a nested route it is named after the whole nesting and gets the parent records, so `/admin/orders/42/messages` calls `order_messages(order)`. On `show` and `edit`, it is the crumb named after the record's model (`post`).
3. The trail Crumbly works out. Its parent levels follow the same rule: your crumb for the parent's model if there is one, or else a level Crumbly builds.

With [`derive_trails false`](https://levups.github.io/crumbly/guide.html#derive-trails), only the first applies.

### Testing your trails

Add one test:

```ruby
# test/breadcrumbs_test.rb
require "test_helper"
require "crumbly/test_helper"

class BreadcrumbsTest < ActiveSupport::TestCase
  test "breadcrumbs" do
    assert_breadcrumbs_valid
  end
end
```

It loads the whole app and reads the source of every crumb, and of the private helpers next to it, without running them or touching the database. It fails when:

- a crumb's parent is not a crumb, or a `_path` or `_url` it calls is not a route helper;
- a `breadcrumb :name` in `app/views` or `app/controllers` names a crumb that no trail class defines;
- a view or another crumb calls a crumb with the wrong number of arguments. gretel ignored extra arguments and passed `nil` for missing ones, but a method raises `ArgumentError`. Calls spread over several lines, or with a splat, are skipped;
- a crumb is never used. A crumb is used when another crumb, a view or a controller calls it (`breadcrumb :name`, `breadcrumb @record`), when a trail Crumbly works out reads it (unless its class sets `derive_trails false`), or when it is named after a model.

A crumb defined twice in the same class is caught even earlier: the class raises `Crumbly::DuplicateCrumb` when it loads.

Outside Minitest, `Crumbly.verify!` runs the same checks. It raises `Crumbly::InvalidTrail` with every problem in one message, and returns the unused crumbs (`["Admin::Breadcrumbs#drafts"]`). Both accept `trail_classes:`, `routes:` and `sources:`, the directories it scans for `breadcrumb` calls.

### Breadcrumbs for search engines

Google can show a page's trail in its results when the page describes it as schema.org structured data. Google needs absolute URLs, so use `_url` helpers in the crumbs of that namespace. They take the host from the current request.

```ruby
module Storefront
  class Breadcrumbs < Crumbly::Trail
    def shop
      crumb "Shop", storefront_root_url
    end

    def category(category)
      crumb category.name, storefront_category_url(category),
        parent: category.parent ? category(category.parent) : shop
    end
  end
end
```

#### JSON-LD

`breadcrumb_json_ld` writes that description for the current trail. Put it in the `<head>`:

```erb
<%# app/views/layouts/storefront.html.erb, in <head> %>
<%= breadcrumb_json_ld %>
```

- Positions start at 1. The last level may have no URL. A level above it without a URL isn't a page, so it is left out.
- Names are plain text. If a label is `html_safe` (an icon, a `<b>`), its tags are removed.
- The JSON is escaped for a `<script>` tag, so a label can't close it.
- A relative URL raises `Crumbly::RelativeUrl` in development and test. In production it is reported to `Rails.error` and the page has no structured data. `Crumbly.raise_on_relative_url` changes this.
- `Crumbly::JsonLd.call(levels)` returns the same data as a hash, if you build the structured data of the page yourself.

### Errors

Every error is a `Crumbly::Error`.

| Error | When |
| --- | --- |
| `Crumbly::DuplicateCrumb` | A trail class defines the same public method twice. It is raised when the class loads: at boot with eager loading, and in any test that loads the class. |
| `Crumbly::UnknownCrumb` | A view names a crumb that doesn't exist, or `breadcrumb @record` or `crumb_for` finds no crumb for the record's model, or the record is `nil`. It is raised in development and test. In production it is reported to `Rails.error`, and the page renders without a trail. |
| `Crumbly::MissingTrail` | A view reads the trail of a controller that has no trail class, found from its module or set with `breadcrumbs_with`. The message names the class to define. |
| `Crumbly::InvalidTrail` | [`Crumbly.verify!`](https://levups.github.io/crumbly/guide.html#tests) found a crumb calling an unknown crumb or route helper, or a `breadcrumb :name` that no trail defines. The message lists every problem at once, and `assert_breadcrumbs_valid` turns it into a test failure. |
| `Crumbly::RelativeUrl` | [`breadcrumb_json_ld`](https://levups.github.io/crumbly/guide.html#storefronts) found a level whose URL is not absolute. It is raised in development and test. In production it is reported to `Rails.error`, and the page has no `BreadcrumbList`. |
| `Crumbly::UnsafeUrl` | A crumb or a `link` gets a `javascript:`, `vbscript:` or `data:` URL, which a browser would run as a script, in any case and with spaces, tabs or control characters around it. It is raised in development and test. In production it is reported to `Rails.error`, and the level keeps its label without the link. |

To choose when an unknown crumb, a relative URL or an unsafe URL raises, set it in an initializer:

```ruby
# config/initializers/crumbly.rb
Crumbly.raise_on_unknown_crumb = true # on staging too
Crumbly.raise_on_relative_url = true
Crumbly.raise_on_unsafe_url = true
```

## Migrating to Crumbly

<https://levups.github.io/crumbly/migration.html>

Crumbly uses the same view helper names as these gems, so an app switches in one go. There is no compatibility layer, and the old gem leaves the Gemfile when the migration is merged.

### From gretel

The idea stays the same: a crumb names its parent. The calls in your views barely change, and `breadcrumb :order, @order` and `breadcrumb @order` work as they did. What changes is `config/breadcrumbs.rb`, which becomes one class per namespace. A converter writes that class for you.

The two gems don't run side by side in production. gretel stays in the Gemfile of the migration branch only, for the comparison in step 2.

#### 1. Convert the breadcrumbs file

```sh
bundle exec crumbly-convert config/breadcrumbs.rb --namespace Admin \
  --output app/breadcrumbs/admin/breadcrumbs.rb --views app/views/admin
```

This writes `Admin::Breadcrumbs`, then prints each thing it left out or couldn't convert exactly, with its line. You can pass several files (`config/breadcrumbs/*.rb`). They become one class, and when a crumb is defined twice the later one wins, as in gretel.

| gretel | Crumbly |
| --- | --- |
| `crumb :key do \|order\| ... end` | `def key(order) ... end`, a parameter tested for nil getting `= nil` |
| `link label, url` | `crumb label, url`; `link label` or `link label, nil` give a level without a URL |
| a second `link` | `links: [link(label, url)]` on the same level |
| `parent :other, order` | `parent: other(order)` |
| `parent record` | `parent: crumb_for(record)` |
| `parent :a` and `parent :b` in an `if`/`else` | `parent: condition ? a : b` |
| `parent :a`, then `parent :b if condition` | `parent: condition ? b : a` |
| `link` and `parent` inside an `if`, `elsif`, `unless` or `case`, modifiers included | one `crumb` call per branch, the statements after the conditional copied into each |
| `t(".x")`, `current_user`: view helpers | `helpers.t(".x")`, `helpers.current_user`; route helpers stay bare |
| `%i[a b].each { \|name\| crumb name do ... end }`, `{a: [:post, Comment]}.each { \|name, (parent, model)\| ... }` | one method per element |
| a local assigned before a crumb reads it: `path = :"admin_#{name}_path"` | copied into each crumb reading it, a literal written in place |
| `label = ->(record) { ... }` at the top of the file, reading no other local | a private method, `label.call(post)` becoming `label(post)` |

Some things are listed for you to convert by hand: a loop over anything but a literal array or hash of symbols, strings, numbers and constants; `link` or `parent` inside a loop or a block; `link` options such as `title:` or `class:`; a crumb named after a Ruby keyword or an existing method (`display`, `test`); and any statement that isn't a crumb, a loop or a local. Comments are kept, above the method they came before.

The converter needs Prism 1.2 or later. Ruby 3.4 comes with it. On Ruby 3.3, add `gem "prism"` to the development group.

#### 2. Compare the trails

While gretel is still installed, your tests can draw every trail with both gems and list where the labels or URLs differ. Keep gretel in the test group with `require: false`. `crumbly/oracle` loads it without gretel's view helpers, whose `breadcrumb` would replace Crumbly's.

```ruby
# Gemfile, on the migration branch
gem "gretel", require: false, group: :test
```

Your views already call `breadcrumb` the way Crumbly expects, so your controller, integration and system tests can do the comparing. With `Crumbly::Oracle.watch` in the test helper, gretel also draws each page the tests render, from the same `breadcrumb` call:

```ruby
# test/test_helper.rb, once the app is loaded
require "crumbly/oracle"

Crumbly::Oracle.watch
Minitest.after_run do
  puts Crumbly::Oracle.differences.to_a, Crumbly::Oracle.redundant_calls.to_a
end
```

`differences` lists each page whose trail changed, with gretel's and Crumbly's side by side. It includes pages with no `breadcrumb` call, which had no trail with gretel and get one now, unless the trail class sets [`derive_trails false`](https://levups.github.io/crumbly/guide.html#derive-trails). gretel shows a crumb's extra links as levels of their own, and the comparison does the same with `links`. A call that gretel can't draw is listed too, with gretel's error. `redundant_calls` lists the `breadcrumb` calls you can delete, because the page gets the same trail without them (none, with `derive_trails false`). `watch { ... }` watches a block only. Parallel test workers each keep their own lists, and `after_run` in the parent process doesn't see them, so run the watched suite with `PARALLEL_WORKERS=1`.

For crumbs that no test renders, `compare` checks the calls you give it:

```ruby
class BreadcrumbsMigrationTest < ActionView::TestCase
  test "Crumbly draws the trails gretel drew" do
    differences = Crumbly::Oracle.compare(view, Admin::Breadcrumbs, [
      [:orders], [:order, orders(:alice)], [orders(:alice)], [:returns], [:returns, customers(:alice)]
    ])

    assert_empty differences, differences.join("\n")
  end
end
```

#### 3. Review the calls in your views

The `--views` option of `crumbly-convert` lists the `breadcrumb` calls that Crumbly may now make unnecessary: `:generic_form` (or `:new`, `:edit`) in new and edit views, `breadcrumb @order` in a show view, and `breadcrumb :orders` in an index view. It doesn't delete anything. Remove a call once its page shows the same trail without it; for the pages your tests render, `Crumbly::Oracle.redundant_calls` tells you which ones. Area prefixes in crumb names (`:admin_order`) can go too, since the namespace keeps the areas apart.

To keep every trail explicit instead, as it was with gretel, set [`derive_trails false`](https://levups.github.io/crumbly/guide.html#derive-trails) in the trail class and keep the calls: a page whose view names no crumb then has no trail.

#### 4. Remove gretel

Remove gretel and `config/breadcrumbs.rb`, and render `breadcrumb_trail` in the layout where `breadcrumbs` was. The [guide](https://levups.github.io/crumbly/guide.html#rendering) has a loop to start from. gretel's rendering options (`style: :bootstrap5`, the separator, `link_current`, semantic markup) become choices in your own markup, and its `structured_data` becomes [`breadcrumb_json_ld`](https://levups.github.io/crumbly/guide.html#storefronts).

Then add the [breadcrumbs test](https://levups.github.io/crumbly/guide.html#tests). It catches the parents, route helpers and view calls that the conversion got wrong, and the crumbs that nothing uses any more.

### From breadcrumbs_on_rails

[breadcrumbs_on_rails](https://github.com/weppos/breadcrumbs_on_rails) builds the trail in controllers. `add_breadcrumb` is called at class level, where a symbol path is called on the controller and `only:` and `except:` pick the actions, then inside actions. Each call adds a level after the last one. `render_breadcrumbs` draws the trail, with a `separator:` or a custom `builder:`.

Crumbly builds the trail from the other end. The view names its last crumb, and each crumb names its parent. Most `add_breadcrumb` calls go away, because `index`, `show`, `new` and `edit` get the same trail from the routes and the record the controller loaded.

breadcrumbs_on_rails

```ruby
class Admin::OrdersController < Admin::BaseController
  add_breadcrumb "Home", :admin_root_path
  add_breadcrumb "Orders", :admin_orders_path

  def show
    @order = Order.find(params[:id])
    add_breadcrumb @order.to_s, admin_order_path(@order)
  end

  def messages
    @order = Order.find(params[:id])
    add_breadcrumb @order.to_s, admin_order_path(@order)
    add_breadcrumb "Messages", messages_admin_order_path(@order)
  end
end
```

```erb
<%= render_breadcrumbs separator: " / " %>
```

Crumbly

```ruby
module Admin
  class Breadcrumbs < Crumbly::Trail
    def root
      crumb "Home", admin_root_path
    end

    def orders
      crumb "Orders", admin_orders_path
    end

    def order(order)
      crumb order.to_s, admin_order_path(order), parent: orders
    end

    def order_messages(order)
      crumb "Messages", messages_admin_order_path(order), parent: order(order)
    end
  end
end
```

```erb
<%# app/views/admin/orders/messages.html.erb %>
<% breadcrumb :order_messages, @order %>
```

index and show find these crumbs on their own. Without `orders` and `order`, they would still get "Orders" and the order's `to_s`, or "Order 42" if Order has none

#### Steps

1. Replace `gem "breadcrumbs_on_rails"` with `gem "crumbly"`.
2. The class-level "Home" becomes `root` in each namespace's trail class. A class-level section crumb ("Orders") becomes a crumb named after the controller, `orders`, but only if the label Crumbly would use (the model's plural name) isn't the one you want.
3. Delete the `add_breadcrumb` calls in `index`, `show`, `new` and `edit`. For other actions, write a crumb and name it from the view with `breadcrumb`.
4. Replace `render_breadcrumbs` with a loop over `breadcrumb_trail`. A custom builder becomes that loop, or your own component.

### From loaf

[loaf](https://github.com/piotrmurach/loaf) adds crumbs with `breadcrumb`, at controller class level (with `only:` and `except:`), inside actions, or in views. Its `breadcrumb_trail` passes each crumb to a block, with its `name`, `url` and `current?`. It decides `current?` by comparing the crumb's URL with the request (the `match:` option).

Crumbly uses the same two helper names, so loaf has to go first. In Crumbly, `breadcrumb` names one crumb instead of adding one, `breadcrumb_trail` returns an array instead of taking a block, and the current level is always the last one.

loaf

```ruby
class Admin::CategoriesController < Admin::BaseController
  breadcrumb "Home", :admin_root_path
  breadcrumb "Categories", :admin_categories_path

  def show
    @category = Category.find(params[:id])
    @category.ancestors.each do |ancestor|
      breadcrumb ancestor.name, admin_category_path(ancestor)
    end
    breadcrumb @category.name, admin_category_path(@category)
  end
end
```

```erb
<% breadcrumb_trail do |crumb| %>
  <li><%= link_to crumb.name, crumb.url %></li>
<% end %>
```

Crumbly

```ruby
module Admin
  class Breadcrumbs < Crumbly::Trail
    def root
      crumb "Home", admin_root_path
    end

    def categories
      crumb "Categories", admin_categories_path
    end

    def category(category, ancestors = category.ancestors.to_a)
      *grandparents, parent_category = ancestors
      crumb category.name, admin_category_path(category),
        parent: parent_category ? category(parent_category, grandparents) : categories
    end
  end
end
```

```erb
<% breadcrumb_trail.each do |level| %>
  <li><%= link_to_unless level.current?, level.label, level.url %></li>
<% end %>
```

show finds the `category` crumb on its own, so the view names nothing

#### Steps

1. Replace `gem "loaf"` with `gem "crumbly"`.
2. Move the controllers' class-level crumbs into each namespace's trail class. "Home" becomes `root`, and a section becomes a crumb named after the controller.
3. Delete the crumbs added in `index`, `show`, `new` and `edit`, and turn the others into crumbs that name their parent.
4. In views, a run of `breadcrumb "Name", path` calls becomes one crumb method, named with `breadcrumb :name`.
5. In the layout, `breadcrumb_trail do |crumb|` becomes `breadcrumb_trail.each do |level|`, and `crumb.name` becomes `level.label`.

## Crumbly Benchmarks

<https://levups.github.io/crumbly/benchmarks.html>

Crumbly against gretel, on the same trails.

### Rendering a trail

`bench/render.rb` renders the same five-level trail (Home > Customers > Alice > Orders > Order 2026-0042) with gretel and with Crumbly, and checks that both give the same output. The `<ol>` row compares gretel's `breadcrumbs(style: :ol)` with a ten-line helper over `breadcrumb_trail`. The JSON-LD row compares gretel's `structured_data(url_base:)`, with paths behind a prefix, and `breadcrumb_json_ld` with `_url` helpers. Both are encoded and escaped the same way.

Ruby 4.0.9, Rails 8.1.4, gretel 5.1.0, Apple M5 (arm64 macOS), median of three runs of benchmark-ips

| Render | Allocations | Time, YJIT off | Time, YJIT on |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| gretel `<ol>` | 345 | 57.6 µs | 35.1 µs |
| Crumbly `<ol>` | 274 | 45.4 µs | 29.8 µs |
| gretel JSON-LD | 268 | 41.3 µs | 25.4 µs |
| Crumbly JSON-LD | 287 | 43.3 µs | 29.5 µs |

Crumbly's JSON-LD is a little slower, mostly because Rails' `_url` helpers are slower than `_path` ones. Building the `BreadcrumbList` from the levels takes 1.7 µs of the difference.

### Running it again

From a checkout of the gem, once with YJIT off and once with it on:

```sh
bundle exec ruby bench/render.rb
bundle exec ruby --yjit bench/render.rb
```

Run each three times and keep the median. The numbers depend on the machine, so compare the two gems on the same one rather than with this table.
